notes:
I've written notes on all seven verses, but some parts of the brief are thin. My search tool hit its usage limit partway through, so I couldn't reach netbible.org's notes, bibleodyssey.org, catholic.com, oca.org, or any Lutheran, Wesleyan or Pentecostal sites. Most of what follows comes from the older commentaries on biblehub.com and studylight.org, plus Enduring Word, Spurgeon, Matthew Henry and bible.org. Where a commentator's view reached me through someone else's page, I say so.

---

## Psalm 110: Notes by verse

### Overview
- **Enduring Word (David Guzik):** It is one of the psalms the New Testament quotes most. It has two movements. First, the Messiah is raised up as king and as eternal priest. Second, he judges the nations. Guzik defends David as author, noting that Jesus himself said David wrote it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-110/
- **Matthew Henry:** He calls the psalm "pure gospel," entirely about Christ. He shows Christ as prophet, priest and king. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_110.cfm
- **Spurgeon:** The subject is "the Priest King." No king of Israel held both offices, and David, from the tribe of Judah, was never a priest. Christ is the whole subject, and David appears only as the writer. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps110.php
- **Luther** called it the "true high main psalm" of Christ. I only saw this second-hand, quoted by S. Conway in the Pulpit Commentary Homiletics. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/psalms/110.htm
- **A non-traditional view (Ellicott):** Ellicott doubts that David wrote it. He argues that Jesus used the beliefs of his day without thereby confirming them. He prefers a setting among the later Hasmonean priest-kings: 1 Maccabees 14:41 calls Simon "high priest for ever." He also thinks the abrupt ending may mean the psalm is a fragment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/110.htm

### v. 1
- **Who is speaking to whom:** Yahweh (the LORD) speaks to the Messiah, whom David calls "my Lord" (Adonai). Guzik takes this as the Father speaking to the Son, and as evidence that the Messiah is divine. Peter uses the verse in Acts 2:34–35, and Paul in 1 Corinthians 15:25. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-110/
- **"Footstool":** Matthew Poole (quoted by Guzik) explains it from the custom of Eastern kings who put their feet on the necks of defeated enemies (Joshua 10:24). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-110/
- **What "sit" means (Matthew Henry):** Sitting is a posture of rest after his work and suffering. It is also the posture of a ruler and of a king who stays on the throne for good. Henry says Jews of old read this verse as about the Messiah. That is why the Pharisees had no answer when Jesus questioned them on it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_110.cfm
- **Why it can't be David himself (Barnes):** "My Lord" means someone of higher rank than the writer. No one on earth in David's time fits that. If David wrote the psalm, it must refer to the Messiah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/110-1.htm
- **Jamieson-Fausset-Brown:** "The LORD said" is literally "a saying of the LORD," a formula used for solemn prophetic statements. Sitting at the right hand means honour and also a share in power. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/110-1.htm
- **Does "until" mean the reign ends? Two readings on the same page:**
  - One commentator says "until" need not mean Christ stops sitting once his enemies are defeated.
  - Another ties it to 1 Corinthians 15. Christ's reign as mediator lasts until the last enemy is destroyed, and then he hands the kingdom to the Father.
  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/110-1.htm
- **Ellicott on "my lord" (adonî):** The word is an ordinary title of respect for a father, brother, prince or king. He lists the candidates people have proposed: the Messiah, David, Solomon, Hezekiah, Joshua son of Josedech, or a Hasmonean priest-king. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/110.htm
- **Bible.org:** If David's son is also his Lord, the Messiah must be both God and man. That is the conclusion the Pharisees refused. The writer treats the psalm's final fulfilment as still future. https://bible.org/seriespage/14-psalm-110-david-s-lord

### v. 2
- **Guzik:** The Messiah's rule reaches beyond Israel to the whole world and over all his enemies. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-110/
- **Pulpit Commentary:**
  - The "rod of strength" means his ruling power, which went out from Jerusalem, as in Acts 1–2.
  - Who says "Rule in the midst…"? Cheyne thinks God is still speaking. Most take it as David calling on the Messiah to reign.
  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/110.htm
- **Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary:** Christ rules a "disputed empire." Many people enjoy his gifts while denying his right to rule. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/psalms-110.html

### v. 3
- **The willing army:** The Hebrew is literally "willingnesses," meaning very willing (Poole). Boice, quoted by Guzik, says Christ's army has no mercenaries or conscripts, only volunteers. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-110/
- **Benson and Poole:**
  - The word can also mean "freewill offerings," which may hint at how New Testament worship differs from Old.
  - "The day of thy power" is when Christ wins people through the preaching of his word.
  - Poole calls the last clause the most difficult and obscure in the whole book of Psalms.
  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/110-3.htm
- **Whose is the "dew of youth"? Commentators split:**
  - *The army.* Maclaren: "youth" is a collective word for young men, a host of young soldiers as fresh and countless as morning dew. Guzik quotes the same reading (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-110/). The Pulpit Commentary says most interpreters take this view. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/110.htm
  - *Christ himself.* The Speaker's Commentary, cited by Pulpit, reads it as the Messiah's own lasting youthful strength. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/110.htm Barnes reads the whole clause as Christ's reign being like a long bright day, with its beginning as fresh as dawn. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/110-3.html
  - *Both.* Spurgeon's sermon says Christ has the dew of his youth "personally, doctrinally, and mystically," because he is surrounded by new converts. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-110.html
- **Gill:** The "dew" is young converts, Christ's lambs, born again by grace and as many as dewdrops. The people were "secretly his" even before they were willing. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/110-3.html
- **Spurgeon:** The people were "given to him of old" and gladly accept his rule when the gospel goes out. "The beauties of holiness" are their priestly clothing, because all his people are priests and kings. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps110.php
- **Biblical Illustrator, on how people become willing:** It describes the human will as bent toward evil. Its point is that people "are made" willing and do not make themselves so. The Lord changes their will. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/psalms-110.html
  - This is the closest I came to a real Protestant disagreement. Gill, Spurgeon and the Illustrator all read the verse as God changing the will. But I could not reach Wesleyan, Methodist or Pentecostal teachers to report their side, so I am not presenting it as a confirmed split.
- **Preacher's Homiletical Commentary:** The verse shows the church has priestly dignity. It also tells the church not to wait idly for special outpourings of the Spirit but to use the power it already has. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/psalms-110.html
- **Translation note:** The NIV footnotes this sentence as having uncertain meaning in Hebrew. https://biblehub.com/niv/psalms/110.htm

### v. 4
- **Guzik:**
  - God's oath makes this as solemn and permanent as possible.
  - Melchizedek (Genesis 14:18–20) was king of righteousness and of Salem (peace) and a priest of God Most High. He blessed Abraham and received a tithe from him. No genealogy is given for him.
  - The verse shows a priesthood separate from Aaron's.
  - Hebrews refers to it five times (5:6, 5:10, 6:20, 7:17, 7:21).
  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-110/
- **Guzik on Hebrews 7:** Simply mentioning another priestly order shows that Aaron's priesthood fell short. Jesus became priest by God's oath, not by family descent. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-7/
- **Matthew Henry:**
  - The oath shows God kept no right to cancel it, unlike Eli's priesthood (1 Samuel 2:30).
  - Melchizedek's order came before Aaron's and is greater, since he was "a priest upon his throne."
  - Christ is priest "for ever" because no other arrangement of grace will follow, and its fruits last eternally.
  
  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_110.cfm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** Melchizedek's was the older priesthood that joined priest and king. Christ is priest for ever because "he ever liveth to make intercession." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/110-4.html
- **Adam Clarke (Methodist):** Christ is a priest for ever as teacher, as the Lamb whose sacrifice takes away sin, and as mediator. He has no successor because he cannot die. Clarke also says the priesthood is eternal in its effects, since the one sacrifice on the cross won eternal redemption. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-110.html
- **Spurgeon:** The oath plus "will not repent" fixes the decree for ever, and this secures the believer. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps110.php
- **Preacher's Homiletical Commentary:** You will look in vain for this kind of authority in any priest except the Son of God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/psalms-110.html
- **Ellicott (critical):** Melchizedek was chosen not to contrast with Aaron but because he was the one example of priest and king in one person. Ellicott links this to the Hasmoneans. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/110.htm

### v. 5
- **The roles reverse:** Maclaren, quoted by Guzik, notes that the King now leaves the throne for the battlefield. Before, he sat at God's right hand; now God stands at his. Kidner says the Lord and his King act as one. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-110/
- **Pulpit Commentary:**
  - "Adonai" here is Jehovah, standing beside the Messiah to protect him.
  - The kings struck down are rulers who opposed the gospel in history: Herod Agrippa, Galerius, Julian.
  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/110.htm
- **Bible Hub's summary** looks instead to a future, long-foretold day of wrath. https://biblehub.com/psalms/110-5.htm
- **Matthew Henry:** The "day of wrath" is the appointed time, when their sins have reached full measure and God's patience is over. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_110.cfm
- **Translation note:** The NIV footnote allows "My lord is at your right hand, Lord" (https://biblehub.com/niv/psalms/110.htm). The NET Bible reads "O sovereign LORD, at your right hand he strikes down kings" (https://biblehub.com/psalms/110-5.htm).

### v. 6
- **Guzik:** The Messiah judges every nation. He links "filling with corpses" to a future end-time battle, but the page text I saw was cut off at that point. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-110/
- **Pulpit Commentary:** It prefers "fill the earth with dead bodies." It also mentions Dr. Kay's reading, "smite him that is head over the wide earth," meaning Satan or the central power of evil. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/110.htm
- **Spurgeon's Treasury:** Christ strikes the greatest powers that resist him, rulers as well as ordinary people. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-110.html

### v. 7
This verse has the widest range of readings.
- **A tired warrior refreshed (Ellicott):** Like Gideon's men, "faint yet pursuing" (Judges 8:4), the victor stops at a stream and then chases on with his head up. https://biblehub.com/psalms/110-7.htm The Hastings *Great Texts* entry reads it the same way: the King leaves the scene as fresh as when the battle began. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hastings/psalms/110-7.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** It takes the literal picture spiritually: the Messiah draws refreshment from truth and righteousness as he advances. https://biblehub.com/psalms/110-7.htm
- **Christ's suffering:** Houbigant, cited by Benson, sees the brook Kidron and the Passion. Poole says the verse stops readers assuming the Messiah would win without suffering. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/110-7.htm A sermon page says Calvin, Hengstenberg and Matthew Henry took the "brook" as God's wrath under the curse of the Law, the cup Christ drank, with the cross's triumphs as the lifted head. This is a second-hand report. https://biblehub.com/sermons/psalms/110-7.htm
- **The Holy Spirit's help:** Hervey and others read the brook as almighty grace or the Holy Spirit, often pictured as water, strengthening Christ for his work. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/110-7.htm
- **Christ sharing our need:** Another preacher on the sermon page prefers this reading: Christ humbled himself to need the same refreshment God gives us. https://biblehub.com/sermons/psalms/110-7.htm
- **Adam Clarke:** Having won, Jesus has sat down on the Father's throne, and his victorious soldiers share it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-110.html
- **Bible Hub's summary:** Humility ("he will drink") leads to exaltation, and his lifted head promises that believers will share his glory (Colossians 3:1–4). https://biblehub.com/psalms/110-7.htm
- **Translation note:** The NIV says the Hebrew meaning of this clause is uncertain. https://biblehub.com/niv/psalms/110.htm

---

## Other views (as far as I could get)
- **Catholic and Orthodox:** I only have a short excerpt of Augustine's exposition. He says Christ, as God's eternal Word, is eternal King. Christ's reign in time, through his human nature, begins with Christians and will never end. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801110.htm I could not reach Catholic or Orthodox material on Melchizedek, the Eucharist, or "from the womb of the dawn."
- **Modern scholarship:** The only modern critical view I found is Ellicott's, given under the overview and verse 4. I could not open the netbible.org notes or bibleodyssey.org.
- **Popular modern teaching (prosperity, word of faith, hyper-grace):** I found nothing on this psalm, so I have left it out.
